title: Number of Valid Subarrays
statement: A contiguous, non-empty subarray of `nums` is **valid** when its first (leftmost) element is less than or equal to every other element inside it. Return how many valid subarrays `nums` has. Subarrays at different positions are counted separately, even if they hold the same values.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct way fixes each start and walks right until a smaller value shows up, which is O(n²). Flip the view and fix the **right end** `j` instead. A start `i` gives a valid subarray ending at `j` exactly when nothing between `i` and `j` is smaller than `nums[i]`. Once a smaller value appears after a start, that start is dead for every later end too. The starts that are still alive therefore form a non-decreasing sequence, and a new value removes the alive starts bigger than it from the top: a monotonic stack. Its size after each step is the number of valid subarrays ending there.

## Approach

1. Keep `stack`, the values that can still begin a valid subarray (non-decreasing from bottom to top), and `count = 0`.
2. For each `value` in `nums`, pop while the top is strictly greater than `value`: those starts now have a smaller element after them.
3. Push `value`; a one-element subarray is always valid.
4. Every value left on the stack is a start whose subarray up to here is valid, so add `stack.length` to `count`.
5. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `nums = [1, 4, 2, 5, 3]`:

- `1`: stack `[1]`, count 1.
- `4`: stack `[1, 4]`, count 3.
- `2`: pop `4`; stack `[1, 2]`, count 5.
- `5`: stack `[1, 2, 5]`, count 8.
- `3`: pop `5`; stack `[1, 2, 3]`, count 11.

The answer is `11`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), since every value is pushed once and popped at most once.
- Space: O(n) for the stack, which keeps everything when `nums` never decreases.

## Pitfalls

- Equal values keep a subarray valid, so pop only on a strictly greater top (`>`, not `>=`); `[2, 2, 2]` must give 6.
- A popped start never returns: one smaller value after it rules out every longer subarray from that start.
- Count per right end by adding the stack size each step; adding only 1 per pushed value would count just the single-element subarrays.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack` | values that can still start a valid subarray, non-decreasing from bottom to top |
| `value` | the current element, the right end of the subarrays being counted |
| `count` | number of valid subarrays found so far |

narration.2: The stack holds the values that can still start a valid subarray, smallest at the bottom.
narration.5: Treat each element in turn as the right end of the subarrays being counted.
narration.6: A start bigger than the new value now has a smaller element after it...
narration.7: ...so it can never start a valid subarray again; pop it.
narration.9: The new value starts its own one-element subarray, which is always valid.
narration.10: Every start on the stack is at most everything up to here, so each gives one valid subarray ending at this value.
narration.12: Each valid subarray was counted once, at its right end.
